pattern: We've already spent {amount} and {duration} on {project}. We can't stop now — we'd be wasting everything we've put in.
explanation: Justifying continued investment by pointing to resources already spent, rather than future prospects, is the sunk cost fallacy.

pattern: I know {project} isn't working out, but after all the {resource} I've poured into it, I can't just walk away now.
explanation: The decision to continue is driven by past investment rather than an honest assessment of future value — the hallmark of sunk cost reasoning.

pattern: The {item} was originally listed at {highPrice}, but now it's marked down to {lowPrice} — what a deal!
explanation: The inflated original price serves as an anchor, making the discounted price feel like a bargain regardless of its actual market value.

pattern: During salary negotiations, the recruiter opens with {lowOffer}. Even after negotiating up to {finalOffer}, the candidate feels lucky, without ever researching the role's typical market rate.
explanation: The initial low offer anchors the candidate's sense of what's reasonable, even though the final number may still be below market rate.

pattern: I tried {sampleSize} {items} from {source} and they were all {quality}, so every {item} from {source} must be {quality}.
explanation: A handful of examples from a small, unverified sample is not enough to justify a sweeping claim about the whole group.

pattern: My {relative} ate {food} every day and lived to {age}, so {food} must not really be unhealthy.
explanation: A single anecdote about one person is far too small a sample to draw a general health conclusion.

pattern: A magazine studies {sampleSize} {group} that became hugely successful and concludes that {habit} is the key to success, without looking at any of the {group} that failed despite doing the same thing.
explanation: Only examining the survivors of a selection process, while the failures that shared the same habits go unseen, inflates how predictive that habit really is.

pattern: Looking only at the {buildings} still standing from {era}, people conclude that construction back then was built to last — ignoring the countless {buildings} from the same era that have long since collapsed or been demolished.
explanation: Only the structures that survived are visible for study, while the many that failed and disappeared are left out of the comparison entirely.

pattern: Convinced that {belief}, {person} notices every instance that supports it, but dismisses or forgets the many times {counterEvidence} happened.
explanation: Selectively registering only the evidence that supports a preexisting belief, while discounting contradicting evidence, is confirmation bias.

pattern: After deciding to buy {product}, {person} only reads reviews that praise it and skips past the negative reviews, feeling reassured about the purchase.
explanation: Seeking out only information that validates a decision already made, while avoiding disconfirming evidence, is confirmation bias.

pattern: After seeing extensive news coverage of {event}, {person} becomes convinced that {event} is common, even though official statistics show it's quite rare.
explanation: Vivid, memorable media coverage makes the event feel far more probable than the actual statistics support — the availability heuristic.

pattern: Right after watching a documentary about {topic}, {person} starts estimating that {topic} happens far more often than it really does.
explanation: The recency and vividness of the documentary makes the topic easier to recall, inflating the perceived likelihood beyond its real frequency.
